card.hook: Here's the honest bit: from The Battery, Lady Liberty is a small figure across open water, not a close-up. But with the harbour and park greenery around her, she makes a lovely scene.
card.stand_here: Stand in The Battery, on the waterfront path at the southern tip of Manhattan (the spot marked 'Statue of Liberty Viewpoint' on the map). The statue is about 3 km south-west of The Battery, so face south-west across the water.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the wide, scenic shot with the trees, water and statue together. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a closer portrait of her. Save 0.5x for the park and waterfront around you.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the statue on one of the intersections, and let the water fill the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: One guide suggests fall and winter sunsets, when the sun can line up behind the statue. At other times of year, check where the light falls on the day.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with Liberty behind you, take the Staten Island Ferry (it boards at Whitehall Terminal) and go up to the open outdoor deck. Stand on the right-hand side as the boat leaves Manhattan, use the front camera at 1x, and let her drift past over your shoulder. She'll be at a distance, not close up. If you visit Liberty Island, the star-shaped base called Fort Wood lets you stand right in front of her.
card.ask_someone: On Fort Wood, the star-shaped base on Liberty Island, ask a passer-by to lie on their back on top of it and shoot upward while you stand in front of the statue, so she towers over you.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual personal photos need no special permission at public viewpoints like Battery Park or the ferry, and personal photography is freely allowed on Liberty Island. Check the official site before you plan a visit to the island itself.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 5x and try to match her pose, with your own 'torch' held high (a coffee cup counts).
card.good_to_know: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from the people of France, designed by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, with an inner metal framework built by Gustave Eiffel. She was dedicated on 28 October 1886. The tablet in her left hand shows the date of the Declaration of Independence, 4 July 1776, in Roman numerals.

card.hook: Here's a secret: almost none of Central Park is natural. The lakes, lawns and woods were built by hand, which is why a stone bridge, still water and trees line up so neatly for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on the shoreline just east of Gapstow Bridge, at the edge of the Pond, just inside the Fifth Avenue entrance near Central Park South (59th Street). Face the bridge, so the Midtown towers and the Plaza Hotel rise up behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the bridge, the Pond and the skyline in one frame. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the towers closer behind the bridge. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground water and trees.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the bridge on a lower third with the Pond filling the bottom and the towers along the top, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when guides say it's less crowded. You'll have a much better chance of a clean shot of the water and the bridge.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and hold your phone a little higher than your face. Turn your back to the view so the landmark sits over your shoulder, and try 0.5x if your phone has it on the front camera so more of the scene fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: Central Park is an open public park. Check the official Central Park Conservancy site before you go for any current closures or rules.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photo and wait for a duck or bird to drift through the frame. Bonus points if it looks like it meant to be there.
card.good_to_know: Central Park was the first landscaped park in the United States. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux won the design competition in 1858 with their 'Greensward Plan'. The first areas opened that same year and the park was finished in 1876. It covers 843 acres, and if you have time left, Bow Bridge over the Lake is a second classic view.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the shoreline just east of Gapstow Bridge, at the edge of the Pond, just inside the Fifth Avenue entrance near Central Park South (59th Street). Face the bridge, so the Midtown towers and the Plaza Hotel rise up behind it.

card.hook: Picture a hall the size of a small village, with hundreds of people crossing it, and one brass clock sitting calmly in the middle like it owns the place. That's the Main Concourse at Grand Central, and it's a lot more fun to photograph than a train station has any right to be.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, inside the Main Concourse of Grand Central Terminal. Face the central information booth and its four-sided brass clock, and keep a little distance from the busiest walking lines.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole hall and its crowds in. Switch to 1x for the booth and clock, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the clock face or the departure boards.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the walls and windows so they stay upright, because this building looks best when everything is straight and symmetrical.
card.best_time: The concourse is usually busy, and trains arrive very often at morning rush hour. Want fewer people in the frame? Try a quieter time outside the commuter peaks. Want lively movement? Go when it's packed.
card.selfie_here: Head outside to the sidewalk along East 40th Street and stand with the terminal's facade behind you. A photographer's blog calls this their favourite way to frame people at Grand Central. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you want more building in the shot, and hold the phone a bit lower so the facade stays over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Pershing Square Viaduct (the overpass at Park Avenue and 42nd Street) to frame you so the Beaux-Arts south facade is in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Phone photos for personal, non-commercial use are fine inside the terminal, with no permit or fee. Professional gear like lights or stabilizers needs a permit from the MTA. It's a working commuter route, so be ready to step aside, and check the official site before you go for opening hours and any access or photography rules.
card.challenge: Take three shots from one spot: the whole hall, the clock, then one tiny detail like a sign or a stranger striding across the floor.
card.good_to_know: Grand Central opened in 1913 on the site of two earlier stations, and it's still a working commuter terminal. It has 44 platforms, more than any other railway station in the world, though they're all underground. About 21.6 million people visited in 2018, not counting train and subway passengers.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: the best Empire State Building photo isn't taken anywhere near its front door. It's taken from Brooklyn, where the Manhattan Bridge wraps around the tower like a picture frame (and yes, other people will be lining up the same shot).
card.stand_here: Stand on Washington Street in DUMBO, Brooklyn, right by the Manhattan Bridge. Face the bridge and look for the Empire State Building sitting inside the arch and ironwork.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the whole bridge arch fits around the tower. If the tower looks too small, try 2x and keep the arch showing at the edges of your picture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, tap the tower, then slide it a little darker so the sky and the pale stone don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, when warm light comes from the west. Take a few shots in case people walk through your frame.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with the building behind you, head to Macy's on 34th Street in Herald Square and stand in front of the store. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more tower in, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by at the corner of 34th Street and Fifth Avenue to photograph you with the whole building in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed at the Empire State Building, so keep your phone in your hand. On Washington Street, take care setting up in the road and have a friend watch for cars.
card.challenge: Take three shots, each with a small step left or right, and find the one where the tower sits perfectly in the middle of the arch.
card.good_to_know: The Empire State Building is a 102-storey Art Deco skyscraper in Midtown Manhattan. Building started in March 1930 and it opened on 1 May 1931, just over thirteen months later. With its antenna it reaches 443 metres, and its pale limestone walls give it a soft, blonde look.

card.hook: Fifty million people a year walk into Times Square, so forget waiting for an empty frame. The crowd is part of the show, and the screens never switch off anyway.
card.stand_here: Head for the spot near Duffy Square: stand about 230 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The billboards stack up on both sides and the street narrows away from you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole scene. Go to 0.5x to fit the billboards on both sides, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single screen above the crowd.
card.make_it_pop: The screens are dazzling, so tap one and slide the brightness down a little (darker) to stop the colours washing out.
card.best_time: Dusk and the hour after it usually work best, when the screens glow and the sky still has some colour. Mornings are generally calmer if you want fewer people in the shot.
card.selfie_here: Climb the red steps above the TKTS booth in Father Duffy Square. They lift you above the crowd, with the whole canyon of screens behind you, and it's free. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the glow fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the pedestrian area between 46th and 47th Streets, face north toward the Coca-Cola sign and shoot wide at 0.5x, with you a few steps in front of them (check the sign is still there when you arrive).
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone strap round your wrist, stay out of the roadway and keep to the pedestrian areas. Events and street works can change what's open, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the same view in a row, then pick the one where the crowd has politely left a gap. Bonus points if it's the one where you're not blinking.
card.good_to_know: Times Square used to be called Longacre Square. It was renamed in April 1904 after The New York Times moved into a new tower here, now known as One Times Square. The New Year's Eve ball drop on that building's roof began in 1907. Up at Duffy Square you'll find statues of Father Francis P. Duffy and George M. Cohan, plus the TKTS booth for same-day theatre tickets.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the spot near Duffy Square: stand about 230 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The billboards stack up on both sides and the street narrows away from you.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so Atlas and the cathedral both fit. Then try zoom 2x to bring the spires in closer behind him, and save zoom 0.5x for when you're down on Fifth Avenue and want the whole white front.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the cathedral, then slide it a touch darker so the pale marble keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the day, when the pavement is quieter and fewer people wander through your shot. Afternoon light is likely to fall on the Fifth Avenue front.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze Atlas statue on the Rockefeller Center side of Fifth Avenue, with the cathedral behind the statue. card.challenge: Line up Atlas and the spires so he looks like he's holding up the cathedral, then take a few frames in a row and see who wins the battle with the people walking through.

The towers on the Fifth Avenue front rise to about 100 metres. It has had restoration scaffolding in past years, so check how the outside looks before you plan your photo.

card.hook: Those pointed stone arches on the Brooklyn Bridge look like they belong on a cathedral, and the web of cables gives you lines to play with in every direction. The best way to see it all at once is from the Brooklyn side.
card.stand_here: Stand in Empire Fulton Ferry Park, right under the bridge's Brooklyn-side approach, and face the bridge so you see it side-on with Lower Manhattan and the river behind it. The Jane's Carousel pavilion often slides into the frame too.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole bridge in profile, then try zoom 0.5x to bring in the carousel pavilion and more of the waterfront. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is perfect for picking out one tower with the cables fanning around it.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour at golden hour.
card.best_time: Golden hour into blue hour is the sweet spot, because the light keeps changing from golden to dusk to night. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone on a wall or rail to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: For a calm selfie with the bridge behind you, head to Pebble Beach (Main Street and Plymouth Street, Brooklyn Bridge Park) and face the bridge with the rocks in front of you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the bridge fits over your shoulder, or grab an outdoor table at Butler Cafe, 40 Water Street, for a seated shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo on the open lawn at Pier 1 in Brooklyn Bridge Park, with the bridge to the north of you, and ask them to step back until the whole bridge is in view.
card.rules_and_safety: The pedestrian walkway gets busy, so expect people to wander through your shot. Night shooting on the waterfront can be windy, so hold your phone firmly and stay aware of your surroundings. Check the official site before you go for any restrictions.
card.challenge: Tuck the carousel pavilion into one side of your frame, then take a second shot with the cables fanning out around a tower, and see which one you like best.
card.good_to_know: The Brooklyn Bridge opened on 24 May 1883 as the first fixed crossing of the East River. It was the longest suspension bridge in the world then, with a main span of 486 metres. John A. Roebling designed it, and his son Washington Roebling and Washington's wife, the engineer Emily Warren Roebling, saw the work through to the end.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Empire Fulton Ferry Park, right under the bridge's Brooklyn-side approach, and face the bridge so you see it side-on with Lower Manhattan and the river behind it. The Jane's Carousel pavilion often slides into the frame too.

card.hook: Everyone heads straight for the stone lions, but you're going to take the quieter route. Look at the library from Bryant Park and it's a pale, calm building rising over green grass and trees.
card.stand_here: Head into Bryant Park and stand on the west side of the park, facing the library. From the park, the library is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the lawn, trees and facade all fit in. Then try 2x to pick out the stonework, and 0.5x if you want a big leafy foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the library along the upper third and let the grass or trees fill the bottom, and keep your phone level so the building's vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stone and a quieter park. Midday sun can flatten the facade.
card.selfie_here: Go to the front steps on Fifth Avenue and stand next to one of the two marble lions. The lions don't block the walkway, so you'll still get the columns and facade behind you. For something more tucked away, step into one of the marble arched niches at the top of the steps. Use the front camera and hold it a little low, so the stone fills the picture over your shoulder.

card.hook: MoMA had over 2.6 million visitors in 2024, so the pavement out front is a lively scene. Skip the hunt for one perfect postcard and shoot the whole street-level buzz instead.

card.good_to_know: MoMA began in 1929, when three friends led by Abby Aldrich Rockefeller started it in rented rooms on Fifth Avenue. It opened just nine days after the Wall Street Crash. It moved to its West 53rd Street home in 1939, and a major renovation finished in 2019 added more gallery space for its 200,000-plus works.

card.hook: In 1902, some New Yorkers looked at this skinny wedge of a tower and nicknamed it "Burnham's Folly" because they were sure it would fall over. It's still here, and it's now one of the most photographed buildings in the city.
card.stand_here: Stand in Flatiron Plaza, on the north side of the building across 23rd Street from the point, with Madison Square Park behind you. Face the narrow peak and you'll see the whole wedge, with Fifth Avenue down one side and Broadway down the other.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole wedge in. If people or traffic push you in close, drop to 0.5x. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the rounded peak and the terracotta detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the peak on the middle line so the two long faces fall away evenly on each side.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 9am, when the plaza is quieter and the eastern face is lit. Midday and weekend afternoons get busy.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sidewalk in front of Eataly beside the 1909 cast-iron Tiffany street clock (5th Ave and 23rd St), so the building rises behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more building in, and keep the tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the triangular plaza across 23rd Street from the building's point, with Madison Square Park behind them, while you stand in front of the point so the full wedge fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: One visitor says shooting from the park across the way lets you get the whole building without passing cars or bikes getting in the way. The building has no public inside or observation deck, so all your photos are from the street. Check for scaffolding or exterior work when you arrive.

card.good_to_know: The Flatiron Building is 22 storeys and 307 feet (93.6 m) tall, and it opened in 1902. Daniel Burnham and Frederick P. Dinkelberg designed it, and the name comes from its resemblance to an old cast-iron clothes iron. The base is limestone and the upper floors are glazed terracotta, and it has since been converted to homes.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Flatiron Plaza, on the north side of the building across 23rd Street from the point, with Madison Square Park behind you. Face the narrow peak and you'll see the whole wedge, with Fifth Avenue down one side and Broadway down the other.

card.hook: Plot twist: the best photo of Washington Square Arch isn't taken at the arch. Walk away from it first, and the whole scene falls into place.
card.stand_here: Start at the Washington Square Arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue, then head south-west to the park. Stand inside Washington Square Park and face the arch, with the fountain in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the arch, trees and park all fit naturally. Try 0.5x for more of the surrounding buildings, but keep the arch away from the edges, where it can look stretched. Tap 2x to pull the fountain a little closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the arch, then slide the picture a touch darker so the bright marble doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Quieter times, like early morning, usually mean fewer people and less traffic in your shot. Pick a clear day if you want to spot the Empire State Building through the archway.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the rim of the central fountain in Washington Square Park and use the front camera. Heads up: from here the arch is in front of you, not behind, and we couldn't find a true arch-behind-you selfie spot. For a proper arch photo of you, try the 'ask someone' shot below.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the fountain area facing north, while you stand in front of the arch with the fountain in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The park has a curfew from midnight to 6 a.m., and drones need a permit. The arch may be fenced off, so a close-up beside or under it might not be possible. Check the NYC Parks site when you arrive. One photographer's blog reports a drug-use problem at the northwest edge of the park and suggests staying in the southeastern section for photos.
card.challenge: Stand on Fifth Avenue, look up through the archway, and see if you can find the Empire State Building. Bonus points if nobody walks into your shot.
card.good_to_know: Washington Square Park is a 9.75-acre park in Greenwich Village, run by NYC Parks. The marble arch is 77 feet (23 m) tall and was modelled on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. Stanford White designed it to replace a temporary plaster-and-wood arch put up in 1889 for the centenary of George Washington's inauguration.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the Washington Square Arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue, then head south-west to the park. Stand inside Washington Square Park and face the arch, with the fountain in front of it.

card.hook: Picture 132 giant concrete flowerpots standing in the Hudson, each one a different height, with a park planted on top. That's Little Island, and it looks a bit like a floating leaf.
card.stand_here: Head to the Northwest Overlook and stand about 30 m north of the numbered pin, right at the phone icon on the map. Face south to take in the lawns and the rising paths.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the lawns, the paths and the shape of the island. Drop to 0.5x for the sweep of the tulip pots and the rolling ground. Use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for flower details and the skyline across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put a winding path along a diagonal so the eye follows it up the slope.
card.best_time: Early morning is calmer, and the evening usually gives softer light over the river. Weekdays are likely quieter than weekends, and the island holds around a thousand people, so wait a moment for a gap.
card.selfie_here: Try near the south entrance, on the West 13th Street side, with the tall concrete tulip columns behind you. A photographer's write-up says they make a clean, modern backdrop. Use the front camera, and check the framing when you arrive, since nobody has described this exact selfie.
card.ask_someone: For a photo with the whole island in view, ask a passer-by at Pier 57 (end of W. 15th Street and 11th Avenue) to take it, as one guide calls that the best place to photograph the island.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public park with its own rules, so check the official site for opening hours and visiting rules before you go.
card.challenge: Find the yellow and gold planting next to the lavender and purple, put it in the foreground, and get the river behind it.
card.good_to_know: Little Island covers 2.4 acres and opened on 21 May 2021, after several years of delays and lawsuits. Heatherwick Studio designed it and Signe Nielsen did the planting. The designers wanted it to look like a floating leaf or a wave.

card.hook: Traffic swirls round a tall monument while the edge of Central Park sits right beside it, and somehow it all works. This is old New York and busy New York in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand near Columbus Circle, about 20 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The circle is about 92 metres across, so you can see the whole shape from here without going any closer.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the circle and the monument together. Go to 0.5x if you want more of the surrounding streets, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the monument's detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the monument in the centre or on a third line, and hold your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer. Around dusk the lights come on, so use night mode if it gets dark.
card.selfie_here: Try the fountain in the middle of the circle plaza, or Merchants' Gate at the Central Park entrance beside the Maine Monument. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little low, and check what's behind your shoulder before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement and use the pedestrian crossings rather than stepping into the road.
card.challenge: Take five frames in a row and see which one has the most interesting traffic going round the monument.
card.good_to_know: The circle was planned as part of Frederick Law Olmsted's 1857 vision for Central Park, and the Christopher Columbus monument was placed at the centre in 1892. The monument is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. It is also the point from which official highway distances from New York City are measured.

card.hook: Lincoln Center is about 440 metres across, so trying to squeeze it all into one photo is a losing game. Start wide, then go hunting for the good bits.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon near Lasdon Colonnade, about 95 m east of the numbered pin, and face west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full width of the plaza and the buildings around it. Then switch to 1x for a more natural look, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the fountain, a facade or people crossing the plaza.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the building edges straight, then tap the brightest building front and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the lit-up facades don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early evening is your best bet, when the lights come on and the sky still has some colour. After dark, switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Go to the Revson Fountain in Josie Robertson Plaza, in front of the Metropolitan Opera House, and pick a spot with the building behind you. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it) and hold it a little low so the Opera House fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official Lincoln Center site before you go for visitor information.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole plaza, then one close-up of a single facade, and see if friends can tell they're the same place.
card.good_to_know: Lincoln Center was built in the 1950s and 1960s as part of a big urban renewal scheme, and its first three buildings opened in 1962, 1964 and 1966. The Charles Revson Fountain opened in 1964 and was redesigned in 2009. The stretch of West 65th Street running through the site is now called Leonard Bernstein Place.

card.hook: Most people hurry into a station staring at the departures board. Here you'll want to stop and look up, because there's a huge glass skylight and it's gorgeous.
card.stand_here: Stand near 8th Avenue, about 35 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. From there you get the long stone front of the old post office, and you can walk the short distance to the entrance for the inside shots.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long stone frontage, and later the glass roof and the full width of the hall. Switch to 1x for natural-looking shots of the clock and people. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the ceiling artwork and the hanging skyscrapers.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the skylight, then slide it a little darker so the glass roof doesn't turn pure white.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when daylight pours through the skylight and shows off the architecture. Wait for a gap in the crowd so a few travellers can walk through the bottom of your frame.
card.selfie_here: Head to the 31st Street entrance and pose next to 'The Hive' sculpture. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the hanging skyscrapers and the hall show up over your shoulder. It's worth a quick check on site that you've got the right spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in the station's public areas, but don't get in the way of operations, other customers, passenger flow or privacy. Opening times and photo rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the four-faced clock and the skylight in one frame, with a stranger striding through the bottom corner, and call it 'Rush Hour in Glass'.
card.good_to_know: Moynihan Train Hall sits inside the James A. Farley Building, the old main post office, which opened in 1914. It was designed by McKim, Mead & White, the same architects as the original Penn Station, which explains the grand stonework outside. The train hall itself opened on 1 January 2021, and its skylight is about 28 metres (92 ft) above the floor.
